titles.l2: Two strange lengths, one ordinary answer

kernelIdea: The irrationals are not closed under addition or multiplication and contain neither 0 nor 1 — they are not a field. But if a is irrational so are −a and 1/a, and a nonzero rational times an irrational is irrational.

kernels.l1: Two strange numbers can add up to a perfectly ordinary one.
kernels.l2: Two numbers that are not pieces can add up to a number that is. So the not-piece numbers do not behave like a tidy number system.
kernels.l3: Adding or multiplying two irrational numbers can land you back among the fractions, so the irrationals are not a tidy system. But the opposite of an irrational is irrational, and so is a fraction times an irrational.
kernels.l4: The irrationals are a strange collection: add or multiply two and you can land back among the fractions, and they contain neither 0 nor 1. But the negative and the reciprocal of an irrational are irrational, and a nonzero fraction times an irrational is irrational.
kernels.l5: The irrationals fail closure but are stable under negation, reciprocal, and multiplication by a nonzero fraction. Each proof is a *suppose not* that leans on closure of the fractions.
kernels.l6: The irrationals are a collection, not a self-contained number system. Their stability properties all follow by contradiction from closure of the fractions.
kernels.l7: The irrationals fail closure under addition and multiplication and contain neither identity, so they form no self-contained number system. Stability under negation, reciprocal and scaling is proved by contradiction from closure of the fractions.
kernels.l8: Sums and products of irrationals can land anywhere, so the irrationals are not closed under arithmetic. That an irrational raised to an irrational can be rational is proved without ever saying which pair works.
